claims.text: Increasing the density and coherence of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries will increase the coating's creep resistance.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Interface-mediated dislocation pinning reduces progressive plastic deformation during continuous high-stress, high-temperature loading.
The proposed baseline is an as-deposited FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating made under standard deposition conditions.
Changing substrate temperature and cooling rate can systematically modify the FCC/BCC phase ratio.
Changing the stated deposition parameters can increase both interphase-boundary density and interphase-boundary coherence.
Creep mechanisms dominate in the proposed range of approximately 1000–1400 K and 2–3 GPa.
Creep behavior is strongly governed by the combined effects of stress and temperature.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries are obstacles to dislocation motion.
A denser and more coherent FCC/BCC interface network constrains dislocation nucleation.
A denser and more coherent FCC/BCC interface network constrains dislocation motion through pinning.
Constraining dislocation nucleation and motion reduces the creep-deformation rate.
At identical test conditions, samples with enhanced FCC/BCC interface density will exhibit lower creep strain than baseline samples.
Samples with enhanced FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit lower dislocation density than baseline samples.
Samples with enhanced FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit reduced dislocation mobility and delayed plastic-deformation onset.
The proposed mechanism applies under sustained high-stress, high-temperature loading, while applicability at lower stress or temperature is unverified.
Diffusion creep or grain-boundary sliding may also influence the measured creep response.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in creep strain and dislocation mobility after increasing interface density and coherence would refute interface-mediated pinning as the dominant creep-resistance mechanism.
